investigation_type: Discovery; real patient-flow decision; native reconstruction; multi-constraint test; criteria reconstruction; cross-system synthesis; real reconciliation test

presentation.investigation_summary:
Hospital patient-flow complexity, multi-system architecture, data-quality problems, human verification, central coordination, prescriptive support, and bottleneck intervention are verified. The final checkpoint could not reconstruct one real event containing multiple systems, conflict or stale data, human reconciliation, explicit trade-off, action, and measured outcome. A ServiceNow-specific gap is therefore not established.

1. Hospital-wide patient flow was identified as a new consequential decision domain.
2. Real patient-flow and bottleneck decisions were reconstructed.
3. Broad coordination, generic resource allocation, and workflow gaps were killed by existing capability evidence.
4. The hypothesis narrowed to cross-system decision synthesis and human reconciliation.
5. Seven-system fragmentation and general data verification were found, but not in one complete event. Prescriptive analytics and human adjudication were counter-evidence to a generic “dashboard only” gap.
6. **Final:** specific cross-system reconciliation opportunity NOT DEMONSTRATED. **KILL.**

key_findings.statement: Seven disconnected systems at Johns Hopkins — Integration problem established generally.
Predictive and prescriptive analytics with recommended bed placement — Weakens assumption that humans manually synthesize everything.
Human adjudication of disputed beds and complex transfers — Human role established, exact burden not.
NHS triangulation and data verification — Workflow-level discrepancy established, not event-level reconciliation.
Hospital U discharge-bottleneck intervention — Real action established, but not multi-system conflict/trade-off/outcome chain.
Required real cross-system reconciliation event — Final hypothesis killed.

decision.decision: **KILL OPP-008.** Preserve the workflow and implementation patterns, but do not create AIL intake or rescue the unsupported residual hypothesis.
decision.reason:
Hospital patient-flow complexity, multi-system architecture, data-quality problems, human verification, central coordination, prescriptive support, and bottleneck intervention are verified. The final checkpoint could not reconstruct one real event containing multiple systems, conflict or stale data, human reconciliation, explicit trade-off, action, and measured outcome. A ServiceNow-specific gap is therefore not established.

The final state distinguishes verified workflow patterns from the missing event-level proof. It does not claim that cross-system reconciliation never occurs.

primary_question:
Whether hospital command centres retain a material, repeatable decision burden when specialized systems are incomplete, conflicting, or context-dependent

The initial question was whether patient-flow coordination exposed a decision domain not covered by ServiceNow. The initial hypothesis was broad: hospital-wide, multi-constraint coordination might need a specialized decision layer. It narrowed to a much stronger requirement: one real event with multiple systems, conflict or stale data, human reconciliation, explicit criteria, trade-off, action, and outcome.

checkpoints.found:
OPP-007 was killed because the supplier-disruption workflow became too well covered by current ServiceNow capabilities.
OPP-008 therefore starts from a genuinely different decision domain:
> **Hospital-wide patient-flow coordination under constrained and changing capacity.**
This is not supplier management, procurement, order management, incident management, or workforce scheduling.
The initial question is:
> **When hospital-wide patient demand, bed availability, staffing, discharge progress, and clinical priorities change simultaneously, how do operational teams decide where capacity should be rebalanced and which patient-flow decisions should take priority?**
The purpose of this checkpoint is not to claim a ServiceNow opportunity.
It is to determine whether the decision problem is real enough to investigate and whether current ServiceNow capabilities already cover it.

A 2026 peer-reviewed multiple-case study examined hospital-wide patient-flow decision making across five leading academic hospitals.
The study used:
- site visits;
- 157 interviews;
- 112 informants.
Source:
https://doi.org/10.1080/09537287.2026.2655748

The study reports that some hospitals moved bed-assignment responsibilities from individual departments into centralized bed-management teams.
This improved the efficiency of patient placement.
Source:
https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09537287.2026.2655748

The study reports that hospitals experience cascading effects when one capacity constraint appears.
Examples include:
ICU STAFF SHORTAGE
↓
OR CAPACITY CONSTRAINT
↓
PATIENT BACKLOG
↓
ED PRESSURE
↓
SYSTEM-WIDE SLOWDOWN
The study describes hospital operations as highly interdependent and notes that a constraint in one part of the system can slow other parts.
Source:
https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09537287.2026.2655748

The study reports that hospitals increasingly centralized coordination because they could bring patients into the system but faced difficulty moving patients through and out of the system.
Source:
https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09537287.2026.2655748

provenance.section: 11. Decision Example — Admission and Discharge Balance

evidence.statement:
A peer-reviewed hospital case study examined allocation of:
- inpatient beds;
- operating theatres;
- nursing staff
to specialties.
The study was motivated by serious bed-utilization problems and admission stops and developed an allocation approach based on patient flows.
Source:
https://doi.org/10.1016/S0377-2217(97)00242-7

Research from Eindhoven University of Technology found that conventional hospital resource allocation can create workload peaks and troughs when capacity coordination requirements are not adequately considered.
The research developed models to support hospital managerial decisions on resource allocation.
Source:
https://research.tue.nl/en/publications/patient-flow-based-allocation-of-hospital-resources-2/

The external evidence shows three properties that make this a potentially strong decision domain:
### 1. Continuous
Decisions occur throughout the day.
### 2. Interdependent
A capacity constraint in one unit can affect other units.
### 3. Decentralized + centralized
Local teams retain clinical/operational knowledge while command centres coordinate system-wide priorities.
Source:
https://doi.org/10.1080/09537287.2026.2655748

evidence.statement:

The study used site visits and 157 interviews involving 112 informants.

The study provides a concrete operational example from Hospital U:
> A patient expected to discharge that day was waiting for a laboratory task. The command-centre manager could identify the patient and barrier and coordinate the laboratory to prioritize the patient.
Source:
https://doi.org/10.1080/09537287.2026.2655748

The study describes command-centre managers and clinical expeditors resolving bottlenecks in patient progression and discharge.
In the documented example, the command-centre manager identifies the barrier and coordinates the laboratory response.

The decision crosses organizational boundaries:
WARD
↓
PATIENT
↓
LABORATORY
↓
COMMAND CENTRE
↓
DISCHARGE
↓
BED CAPACITY
The command centre does not merely record the barrier; it coordinates action across departments.
Source:
https://doi.org/10.1080/09537287.2026.2655748

14. Independent Real-World Case — Dynamic Bed Capacity

evidence.statement:
A hospital bed-management study used one year of patient-flow data and discrete-event simulation to evaluate emergency and elective patient flows.
The study used multiobjective optimization to identify Pareto-optimal bed-allocation solutions under conflicting objectives.
Source:
https://doi.org/10.1111/itor.12360

The documented example supports:
### Time
The discharge is expected today.
### Dependency
A laboratory task remains outstanding.
### Resource ownership
The laboratory controls the outstanding task.
### Patient-flow objective
The task must be addressed to support the planned discharge.
### Organizational coordination
The command centre coordinates across departments.
Source:
https://doi.org/10.1080/09537287.2026.2655748

The documented case explicitly demonstrates one action:
PRIORITIZE THE OUTSTANDING LABORATORY TASK
Other actions are logically conceivable:
1. Prioritize the lab task
2. Delay discharge
3. Escalate to another responsible team
4. Re-sequence other work
5. Change downstream bed planning
evidence.classification: Only **Action 1** is directly supported by the case.
